new_statements.quote: The basic stem-level melodies, which can be realized on stems or words of variable syllable count, are {H}, {L}, {HL}, and {LHL}. The only syllable-level tones are H, L, and <HL> (i.e. falling). [p. 51] ... Because of their prosodic heaviness, gà:-y-ndì and gà:-n-dòŋ in particular have some phonetic stress on their first syllables that can sound like H-tones. However, in my current interpretation they have the same (low) tones as in bà:-y-ndì+H 'our share', rather than the H-tone of má:y-ndì+H 'our name'. [p. 258]
new_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2014. Grammar of Humburi Senni (Songhay of Hombori, Mali). May 2014 version. Language Description Heritage Library, MPI-EVA Leipzig / Univ. of Michigan Deep Blue (hdl 2027.42/117647).
new_statements.locator: §3.9.1, p. 51 (PDF p. 64); incidental stress remark §5.9.4, p. 258 (PDF p. 271)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Humburi Senni is a tone language (syllable tones H, L, falling <HL>; stem melodies {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LHL}; no rising tone). The grammar's 449 pages contain no stress or accent section and state no word-stress rule; the only mention of stress is an incidental note that two prosodically heavy locative pronominals carry phonetic stress on their first syllable that can be mistaken for H-tone, plus 'rhetorical stress' (intonational emphasis) on kûl 'all'.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress system described). Phonetic first-syllable stress noted only for gà:-y-ndì, gà:-n-dòŋ (p. 258).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonology; the stress remark concerns word-internal phonetic prominence in two inflected postpositional forms, and the kûl 'stress' is phrase-level emphasis/intonation (pp. 83, 100, 241).
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2014 describes Humburi Senni (HS) of Hombori and surrounding villages, Mali = humb1243 exactly. Hacquard & Dupuis-Yakouba 1897 (in the Glottolog list for humb1243) actually describes Songhay from Timbuktu to Say (Koyra Chiini koyr1240 / Zarma zone), not Hombori, and says nothing about accent placement.

sources.locator: §3.9.1, p. 51 (PDF p. 64); incidental stress remark §5.9.4, p. 258 (PDF p. 271)
sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology has no stress/accent section; §3.9 Tonology (p. 51) sets out a tone system with syllable tones H, L, <HL> and stem melodies {H},{L},{HL},{LHL}. The word 'stress' occurs only incidentally: p. 258 (§5.9.4) notes that prosodically heavy locative pronominals gà:-y-ndì, gà:-n-dòŋ 'have some phonetic stress on their first syllables that can sound like H-tones'; p. 100 says kûl 'all' is 'nearly always rhetorically "stressed"' (treated as intonational). No statement of a word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Hacquard, Augustin & A. Dupuis-Yakouba. 1897. Manuel de la langue soñgay parlée de Tombouctou à Say dans la boucle du Niger. Paris: J. Maisonneuve.
sources.note: No accent/phonology section; preface (p. iii) only remarks that the ear must catch 'les syllabes accentuées'; one line that 'l'intonation de la voix suffit souvent à indiquer le sens interrogatif'. Describes Timbuktu-to-Say Songhay (Koyra Chiini/Zarma zone), not Hombori.
